tooltip: The place where I was born and spent about half of my life. It is the place I return to when I want to feel where I come from.

My first move away from the place where I was born, away from my roots and my family. At 17, I was completely alone and felt incredibly sad. For the first month, I did little but cry. Yet for the rest of the days, months and years I spent in Saint Petersburg, I was happy. Now, 18 years later, I see this move as one of the best decisions of my life.
The start of my PhD programme, and the reason I had to move to Moscow. Too much movement, speed and noise. After the quietness of smaller cities, Moscow felt overwhelming.

I moved back to Saint Petersburg, where I felt a sense of belonging that I had never really found in Moscow. I learned that the environment around you shapes your life more than you realise. It is easier to build a life when the place itself feels right.

A new chapter of my life, bringing an experience I could hardly have imagined: learning to live and work in an international community. Somewhere along the way, I started to feel less like someone from a city written in a passport and more like someone from planet Earth.

Another chapter in my life. It was shorter than I had planned and very different from what I had imagined, as it coincided with one of the most challenging periods of my personal life. Yet it taught me that sometimes it is worth closing a book when you no longer like the story.
A period of trial and error in trying to integrate into French life. In the end, I had to accept that my own views can change tooб and find a new way forward.
I spent every summer here with my grandmother, while my parents usually came only for the weekends. For a child, the Volga and our family summer house felt like the whole world.

A place where part of my family comes from. We visited several times throughout my childhood and later life. I associate it less with a particular event than with the feeling of being somewhere that existed in my family long before I did.

A children’s summer camp focused on mathematics and IT. Not much learning came from it, but many unforgettable emotions did. It was one of the first places where being away from home alone felt exciting rather than frightening.

A trip to Saint Petersburg with my sister to apply to Saint Petersburg State University and see the city. Yes, back then, it was impossible to apply online. It was my first time travelling so far from the region where I was born. I was overwhelmed by the scale and beauty of the city, and immediately knew that I wanted to live there.

My first vacation by the sea, and the first time I ever swam in the sea. I travelled there with my mom by train. It took us two days to get there from Kazan. At the time, the journey itself felt like part of the adventure.

The first time I got badly sunburned and stayed up raving at night. I remember the amazing nature, kind people and grapefruits. The first fresh figs I ever ate, picked straight from a tree. But I also remember a cannon left by the side of the road, almost exactly where it had been left during the civil war of 1992-93. That contrast between everyday beauty and the traces of conflict stayed with me.

A reunion of former classmates from Kazan School, while visiting one of them at Moscow State University. I remember going up to the 32nd floor of the University and gazing on the city about 230 metres above the Moskva River.

The first stop of the Work & Travel USA program. My friend and I were walking in New York at night. The city was permeated with the smell of fast food and burned oil. There wasn't a single corner among the skyscrapers where you could escape it.

The second stop of my American journey. On our first day, we went swimming in the Atlantic and someone suddenly yelled, Shark! I was terrified. A few weeks later I was confidently walking along the highway, stepping over crocodile carcasses. Somewhere between the shark and the crocodiles, the American South stopped feeling like a distant world and became normal to me. The trip changed how I saw cultural difference: things can be simultaneously strange and familiar.

To get to this place, we had to drive across a half of the country, from Florida to South Dakota. While selling T-shirts and souvenirs to bikers at the annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, I realized that you really shouldn’t judge people by their covers.

This is where I became fascinated by the history of human civilization, standing among the ruins of Knossos. It was the moment when I first touched culture rather than simply looking at it in an art book.

My first serious, adult economic conference. Three days of listening, meeting people and discussing real research made me realise that I was fascinated by this world. I began to see the importance of research, and of understanding issues that matter to society.

Student life is not complete without an Erasmus experience. Mine happened here. So many cultures to communicate with, so many people to meet, and some of the best years of my youth. Even though it lasted only four months, it felt like a whole lifetime.

I made many trips to Berlin while I was on Erasmus in Germany. I couldn’t leave them out: Berlin showed me what freedom feels like, what it means to feel accepted even when you are different, and what it means to trust life.

A short MBA programme in Paris, where, alongside learning how to run a business in Europe, I discovered the French wine industry and did my first wine tasting. That experience stayed with me and sparked an interest that would last for years.

A treat to myself, nothing else. Just two days on the French Riviera between studies. Yet, back then, I made a wish to live there. Ten years later, I came back and bought an apartment in the region. Sometimes wishes do come true.
One trip with my Erasmus friends, full of laughter, sun and pleasure. A final celebration of our time in Germany. It left me with one lasting thought: my friends can come from anywhere in the world.

I spontaneously visited a friend as soon as the idea came to me. I have tried to carry that attitude with me ever since: sometimes there is no need to postpone things. The moment you want to do something can be the right moment to do it.

I joined a group of Russians from my former faculty whom I had seen only a few times in the corridor and had never really spoken to. We spent about ten days together in Amsterdam and Barcelona, living under one roof, making plans and finding common ground. It felt less like a holiday and more like a training course in communication.

A cultural immersion through Gaudí’s masterpieces: Sagrada Família, Sant Pau, Palau de la Música Catalana and Fundació Joan Miró. For a few days, the city felt like one enormous encounter with art and architecture.

Out of curiosity, I went to a student UN game, representing North Korea. Yes, quite an experience. Three years later, I received a positive reply to my application for a UN student internship, the opportunity that eventually became eight years of living in Geneva. Another reminder that sometimes a small step can lead somewhere you could never have predicted.
Another student UN game. Another experience of defending a position I hardly agreed with myself.
A trip back to Berlin, just to recharge my battery. There are only a few places in the world where I can do it as quickly and naturally as in this city.

I will never forget a candlelit medieval tavern where the staff stayed in character, food was served without cutlery, and you could get a hearty elk soup. It was quite an immersion into medieval times.
The Bremen Town Musicians sculpture, featuring the characters from a fairy tale I loved so much as a child. Seeing them unexpectedly in Riga felt like meeting a piece of my childhood again.

I got poisoned by a traditional dish that was simply too fatty for me. It was the only time in my life so far that I have been poisoned by food while travelling. Since then, I have been much more careful with it. And somehow, this is the only memory I have of Vilnius.
Soviet-style architecture and an almost excessive sense of order. Everything felt so controlled that, instead of making me feel comfortable, it became almost suffocating.
So much nature around the city. Helsinki felt almost built into it, rather than having nature added around it.
The Swedish approach to life seemed to be everywhere. IKEA probably could not have come from anywhere else.
Without planning it, I came back to this city just four months later, seeing it first covered in snow and then under the sun.
A reunion with my Erasmus friends. We remembered the nice moments, but also realised how much we had already changed in just one year.
Beautiful architecture, but a feeling of insecurity that I had not expected. The contrast between the beauty of the city and how unsafe I felt there was shocking to me.
The unforgettable works of Matisse, which expanded my understanding of colour and the simplicity of form.
Visiting the UN building. Somewhere during this trip, I made the decision that I wanted to work there.

We got to the bus stop too late, and couldn't leave the place before the night, ending up walking in the city the whole night. Trips require flexibility, and sometimes you just have to accept that things will not go as planned.
Cold, and somehow the same coldness in the modern architecture. I had the feeling that no other kind of architecture could fit this place.

A trip with a medical purpose related to a family member. It was emotionally very difficult, but it became part of an experience that deeply affected me and changed both my personality and the course of my life. I couldn’t leave it out.

I joined a group heading towards Mount Elbrus. We walked with tents and food for ten days, reaching 3,500 metres, and then spent 18h climbing towards the summit at 5,500 metres and back. I think I needed this trip to forget one of the most difficult years of my life, something that could wake me up and remind me how beautiful life can be.
That was a marathon era in my life, I guess as in lives of many people. This trip had a purpose to run a half marathon in Moscow. Who wasnt there.
What I remember most are the unbelievably blue lakes I had never seen before, and blueberries growing everywhere.

My first five-day trip on a yacht. I agreed to go without thinking twice. Somehow, I ended up falling in love with the feeling of the wind and the absolute freedom. No land in sight, just me and the sea.
My first trip abroad completely on my own, with no purpose, just going with the flow. It was only a couple of days, but for me it was a big step.

My first trip to a developing country. I landed in Colombo, walked out of the airport and started to cry. I didn’t even want to stay for a day. I had to pull myself together and give the trip a chance. In the end, after a lot of adjustment and acceptance, I learned so much about the culture, local people and the economy I had previously known only from statistics and textbooks.

Learning to surf along the coast, keeping my balance on the waves and trying not to think about sharks. Then, at the end of the trip, I was bitten by a monkey and spent some unforgettable hours in a tiny medical centre debating with a local doctor whether I needed a rabies vaccine.

Seeing how ordinary people lived, visiting tea plantations and reflecting on local beliefs at the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic. It was one of my first experiences of seeing an economy and a culture from the inside rather than through data.

What was supposed to be an ordinary trip to apply for a Swiss visa ended with me entering the Swiss consulate with a black eye and a sunburnt nose. I still remember the nice lady checking my identity, looking at me, then at the photo of the 'good girl' in my passport, and smiling.

I came back to the place where I had once been lost and had to spend the night walking around the city. This time, I saw it differently, not as a tourist passing through, but with the feeling of being a citizen.

A trip with a Moldovan family I had met while living alone in Switzerland. They had supported me when I was far from my own family, and this trip gave me the feeling of being part of a family again, even so far from home.

My first real holiday after a very long and difficult period at work. I was struggling to find my place in an international organisation, not knowing whether I would stay or leave, or even where I belonged. For a few days, I could finally breathe out.
I joined a group of CERN engineers for a trip to Punta Helbronner in the Italian Alps. What I remember most is the sight of those enormous white mountains in the middle of summer.
A visit to the annual Jazz Festival, surrounded by music, summer and happy people. I was in love with my new life then, and seemed to see only the positive in everything around me.
A small trip into what felt like typical Swiss life: quiet, orderly and somehow completely different from everything I had known before.
Another day travelling alone, seeing a new city and its architecture. At that age, I drank new places in big gulps.
I might have had Stendhal syndrome from everything I saw, or perhaps it was simply the August heat. Either way, Florence was almost too much to take in.
At 26, I finally discovered what real Italian pizza is, and I couldn't get enough of it. Every single evening of that trip ended by the sea, with a pizza in my hands.

When I arrived, my partner unexpectedly knocked on my hotel door and left me speechless. From that moment, I started looking at him differently, and at our future with new possibilities. I definitely don’t remember much about the city.
An amazing day with my partner that we still return to in our memories. He once told me that he had never seen me happier.
Visiting a friend from Moscow and seeing each other on the other side of Europe. It felt strange, as if we were meeting again, but in another life.
Fighting my fear of heights while crossing one of the longest pedestrian suspension bridges in the world: 85 meters above the ravine. Sometimes the only way through a fear is to keep walking.
Joining a group of people and realising that I probably would have been better off staying at home. Sometimes that is also part of the experience.

I finally went to learn to snowboard, something I had dreamed about for years. In the end, I remember sitting on a beginner’s green slope and crying from the pain in my body while three-year-olds glided past me as if they had been born on a snowboard.
A road trip with a group of friends, and one very serious concern: whether we would actually make it back alive, judging by the way one of the guys was driving.
Meeting my mother a year after I had left Russia for Geneva. I don’t think this place needs any other explanation.
So much mineral water and so much gas that I left the place feeling like a bubble.
Visiting a place where I had once felt very happy, long before.
My first visit to my future family-in-law, and my first glimpse of traditional central Spain. And on the way, stealing my boyfriend away for a New Year’s trip.
My first long trip with my future husband. Seven years later, we would come back to this island to get married.
A few days in a tent in front of a crystal-blue lake, perfectly flat and impossibly calm.
A trip to visit a school friend, ten years after we had finished school. It was strange to realise how much life could happen in between.
Escaping for my birthday and disappearing somewhere in the Swiss Alps. Sometimes I just needed to get away.
I went to study Spanish, but the real purpose was to become part of the local life for a while: speaking the language, meeting people and trying to understand the culture from inside.
Showing Switzerland to my mother. Seeing a place through the eyes of someone discovering it for the first time made me look at it differently too, and notice again where I was.
A very cosy summer trip. The kind of place and memory I return to in my mind when life gets turbulent.
A very challenging work trip, but also the moment I realised that this was exactly the part of my job I enjoyed most.
Representing the work of my team at a conference. Yet my strongest memory is much less professional: eating freshly caught oysters at a fish market.
I went to Moscow to take exams for my PhD, and ended up facing family difficulties again. Another reminder that, somehow, Moscow never seemed to bring me much luck.
It felt strangely like coming back to the Soviet Union, not the one I knew, but the one I had heard about in my parents’ stories.
Very local Cuban life: salsa playing every evening, riding horses to visit coffee and tobacco farms, making agreements and then discovering the next day that the deal had somehow been broken.

I watched the woman in the house where we stayed slowly prepare and serve everything. She seemed completely unbothered by how much time it took. It taught me to stop being so nervous about losing time.
We met an european woman, who shared with us her story about how she had left IT to open a flower shop. I caught myself thinking how much I envied her freedom.
The mausoleum of Che Guevara. Seeing how one person could change the history of an entire country.
A few days by a crystal-clear ocean, mostly to rest after everything else we had seen on the trip.
An ideal winter escape: sunny days, skiing and being with someone you love.

Visiting my future family-in-law during carnival season and seeing them in costumes they had made themselves: Matryoshka dolls, the Snow Maiden and a typical young Russian man from a national fairy tale. A very Russian memory in central Spain.

I came to see the result of a year’s work building the family house that I had supervised remotely. It was satisfying to finally see the physical result of my efforts, much more tangible than an article in a journal or a written report.
Waking up in a local house at sunrise, in the middle of vineyards, with morning haze hanging over the hills. That trip I reflected a lot about what's the life purpose.
I was surprised by how much authentic local character had been preserved with such elegance and care. It felt completely different from much of the rest of Europe.
I was surprised by the beauty of the city. I arrived with almost no expectations or plans, which probably made the surprise even better.
Dissolving into crystal-clear, warm water, barely feeling any difference between the temperature of the sea and my own body.
Walking through the layers of past civilisations and feeling how much history can accumulate in one place.
A typical holiday where you become a museum rat, spending the days moving from one museum to another and taking in more art than you can possibly process.
Spending New Year’s away from the noise, chaos and traditions. Just a few quiet days instead.
Seeing deer come right up to the place where we were staying. I found it incredibly touching.
Discovering some of the most beautiful calas I had ever seen and feeling completely connected to nature.
Two days in Rome, ending with no feeling left in my legs but a head full of stories about the beginnings of our civilisation.
Walking about 20 kilometres with no real plan: "Let’s see if we can get to that point, and then decide whether to go back or keep going."
Celebrating my love for the Swiss Alps on Valentine’s Day.
Exploring Alsace through its wines: Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir and Sylvaner. A very enjoyable way to discover a region.
Just a couple of days to merge with the dynamism of a big city again.
Never quite knowing whether it was going to rain or whether I should put sunscreen back on my nose.
Everyone kept telling us that we should visit this place. So we did.
Somehow, the folder from this trip is full of photos of our dog sitting under a sun umbrella and looking at the sea.
Participated in a wine course, learning about this fascinating sector, tasting wines and getting deeper into something I had been interested in for years.
A trip alone with my dog, simply getting to know the city at my own pace.
Showing Saint Petersburg to my partner, drinking hot chocolate and walking around in minus 20°C.
A few days at a spa in the Alps. Perhaps the best holiday my body had ever had.
A French language course. Again another attempt. Six years of my efforts to learn the language.
Visiting a place I love again, walking the same streets and feeling the same vibe.
A family trip to the place where my husband’s grandmother spent an important part of her life. Not every trip becomes a favourite memory, but it still becomes part of the map.
Failing a wine exam to get certified, and as a treat to myself eating a burger with two layers of meat. Somehow, the burger is what I remember.
Stones, wind and landscapes that looked almost like my idea of Mars. The volcanic landscape felt completely alien.
Lanzarote, the place where I finally fell into the arms of the Canary Islands.
I remember Bordeaux as surprisingly humid and dark, absolutely nothing like what I had imagined.
Discovering the Azores through dramatic landscapes, fishing villages, green pastures and enormous waterfalls. A place that felt almost unreal in its intensity of green.
Tomorrowland: telectronic music, enormous digital worlds and complete immersion in an aesthetic that felt like a glimpse into the future.
Paragliding over the Alps. An unbelievable rush of emotion, difficult to describe in words.
I was already feeling that a difficult period of my life was coming. Somehow, even then, I sensed a storm approaching and felt afraid that these might be the last days of calm.
Hiking through the forest to a field of cooled lava, walking through a landscape shaped by something that had once been fire.
Huge waves, wild ocean and an almost empty beach. Just as it should be.

Watching a group of monkeys run towards tourists’ things to steal potato chips, only to struggle with opening the bag. For a moment, I could almost see how we humans behave in the same way: running to get something, only to realise that once we have it, we genuinely don’t know what to do with it.

I couldn’t quite understand how we had reached the point of making a business out of preserving wildlife. If the purpose is to leave animals in their natural environment, perhaps we should leave them alone, rather than bring tourists into protected places to see them.
Walking along Bahía Ballena and enjoying the last days of the trip. Yet I was already uneasy about going home, knowing that the calm of the holiday was coming to an end.
A short trip to explore a possible next chapter. More of a reconnaissance trip than a holiday, walking around, looking, comparing and trying to understand what life here might feel like.
Another reconnaissance trip, this time staying long enough to experience the rhythm of everyday life rather than simply passing through.
One more stop in the search for a place that could become home. By this point, I was no longer simply travelling through southern France, I was trying to imagine myself living there.
I wanted to see my family and return to the roots I had left behind sixteen years earlier. Some places remain part of you even after you leave them.

Spending a month reformating our apartment while trying to navigate everyday life in a new place, including a long-running battle with a local French restaurant over the noise. Quite a practical training in integration.

My partner and I decided to organise our wedding and started looking for a place. Living in the Canary Islands, Tenerife was the obvious first choice, the island where we had spent our first holiday together eight years earlier.
A trip back to Tenerife to see the famous carnival, while also dealing with some private matters. Life rarely separates the beautiful things from the difficult ones.

I deliberately left several medical trips off this map. This one, however, belongs here. These few days marked one of the biggest transformations in my life: I realised I needed to search for a different purpose, even when I could not yet see what it was.
Our wedding. Family, friends and a place that had already been part of our story for years.
Another medical trip. I came back with little more than hope in my heart, but sometimes hope is enough to carry you forward.
Visiting a place I had first discovered on a board game, rather than knowing it as a real city. Strange to finally find the place from the game in the real world.
Another birthday, and as always, I needed an escape. This time I chose a place where I had already been happy once. Perhaps I was trying to touch that happiness again.
I needed a change from a small city, and this option came up. I said yes without thinking too much.
Returning to my roots again. With time, I notice that they have started calling me more and more often.
